title: The impact of bad posture on quality of life and lifting form
summary: NH argues that there is a universal proper static posture, cued by imagining a thread pulling the head up. Poor posture is a vicious circle of hanging on the skeleton while the supporting muscles atrophy, and it carries over into lifting as shoulder, lower back and disc problems.
claims: There is a universal proper static posture everyone should adopt
Non-lifters mostly get injured in everyday dynamic tasks like lifting boxes or moving couches, which we do far more often than lifting
Cue posture by imagining a thread through your body pulling the top of your head up and straightening the spine
Don't overextend into a rigidly straight spine; its natural curves absorb shock
Standing for long periods with locked knees cuts circulation and can make you faint
Keep a slight natural bend but fight the pull of the head and arms rather than surrendering to it
Holding good posture takes abdominal strength, a strong upper back and traps to keep the shoulders back and down, and neck muscles to keep the head up
Bad posture is a vicious circle: the more you hang on your skeleton and tendons, the less the postural muscles work, the weaker they get and the worse posture becomes
Cues: chin up, eyes forward, chest out, shoulders back, whether sitting or walking; everyday posture is training for your body
Many non-lifters get back and neck pain because atrophied muscles leave the skeleton to bear the load
Long hours at school desks train people into a rounded posture
People who slouch carry it into the bench and deadlift, causing shoulder problems, lower back pain and disc injuries
He strongly disagrees with the current view that bad form and bad posture don't exist
People with lower back injuries tend to round even more to protect them, which you should avoid
Deadlift with a neutral spine, avoid knee valgus in squats, and keep the shoulders tucked back on bench
Neck curls help fix forward head posture by strengthening and building the neck
Thoracic rounding leads to lumbar rounding, so keep the shoulders back and the thoracic spine straight
exercises: strengthens the neck to correct forward head posture
